lesson.title: Fully Independent Copies: The deepcopy() Function
lesson.summary: copy.deepcopy() recursively copies a list and every nested list inside it, producing a result that shares no mutable objects at all with the original.
lesson.body:
The shallow copy chapter showed the gap in copy(), list(), and slicing: they duplicate the outer list, but nested lists inside stay shared, so editing an inner list through the copy silently edits the original too. When that shared connection is not what you want, Python's copy module offers deepcopy(), a function that walks through a list recursively and copies every nested list, and any nested list inside that one, and so on, so the result shares nothing mutable with the original at any depth.

Using deepcopy() requires importing the copy module first, since it is not one of the automatic list methods like copy() is, it lives in Python's standard library instead.

```python
import copy

matrix = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
deep = copy.deepcopy(matrix)
deep[0][0] = 99
print(matrix)
print(deep)
```

This prints:

```
[[1, 2], [3, 4]]
[[99, 2], [3, 4]]
```

Compare this directly to the shallow copy example from the last chapter, where the identical looking edit, changing index [0][0], leaked through and changed matrix as well. Here it does not, because copy.deepcopy(matrix) did not just copy the outer list and reuse the same inner list objects. It built brand new inner lists too, [1, 2] and [3, 4] each got their own independent copy, so deep[0] and matrix[0] are two separate objects with equal contents rather than two names for one object. Editing deep[0][0] only ever touches deep's own copy.

Deep copying is more expensive than shallow copying, since Python has to visit and duplicate every nested object rather than just the top level list, so it is not something to reach for automatically on every list. The decision comes down to one question: does this list contain other mutable objects, like nested lists, that you need to change independently of the original? If the list only holds simple immutable values like numbers or strings, a shallow copy already gives you full independence, since there is nothing nested to share in the first place, and copy() or list() is the simpler and faster choice. Deep copy earns its place specifically when nested mutable structure is present and true independence at every level actually matters.
